SK2183 A static member is reached through a type that inherits it

The qualifier names a derived type and the static member is declared on a base, so the line reads as though the derived type owned state that is shared with every other type in the hierarchy.

CategoryCorrectness
Default severitysuggestion
ScopeSemantic
Needs a compilationyes
Runs under --load=looseno
Cached per fileyes
Fixyes, safe
Language version floor—
Since2.0
ReSharperAccessToStaticMemberViaDerivedType (resharper_access_to_static_member_via_derived_type_highlighting)

Why

Leaf.Count and Root.Count are the same slot. Written the first way the line says otherwise: it reads as Leaf's counter, and the reader who goes looking for the declaration on Leaf does not find it. The mistake costs something the day a second type derives from Root and the two are found to share the value nobody thought they shared, and again the day Count moves — because a qualifier naming a type that does not declare the member is the one reference the compiler will happily keep resolving to somewhere else. ⚠ Neither the compiler nor the SDK reports it, and that was probed rather than assumed. At AnalysisMode=All with EnforceCodeStyleInBuild, Leaf.Count, Leaf.Read(), Leaf.Limit and Leaf.Total produce nothing; CA1000 and IDE0002 were each raised to warning and stayed silent on all four.

Example

Instead of:

class Root { public static int Count; }

class Leaf : Root { }

int Read() => Leaf.Count;

Write:

class Root { public static int Count; }

class Leaf : Root { }

int Read() => Root.Count;

The ReSharper mapping

⚠ The export sets resharper_access_to_static_member_via_derived_type_highlighting to warning and this rule defaults to suggestion, so reading the ReSharper key changes behaviour. The lower default is deliberate: the two spellings resolve to the same member, so nothing the program does is wrong — what is wrong is what the line says. docs/plan/16 § Q5.

When it does not fire

⚠ The accessibility guard is defensive and the shape it guards against could not be constructed, which is a refutation rather than a claim. The intended case was a public type deriving from a less visible base, whose declaring type the fix could not then name — but CS0060 makes a base less accessible than its derived type a compile error, and a base in an assembly the caller does not reference is CS0012, so neither reaches an analyzer. The check is kept because it costs a comparison and because it is the one call in this batch that can throw: Compilation.IsSymbolAccessibleWithin raises for a within argument that is neither a type nor an assembly, so the argument is narrowed to an INamedTypeSymbol before the call and falls back to the assembly where there is none. There is no fixture for it, deliberately — the fixture written for it turned out to prove the opposite and was replaced. ⚠ Only fields, properties, methods and events. A nested type reached through a derived type — Leaf.Nested — is not a static member access and the C# rules for it are different; a constant is included, because a const is a static member for this purpose and moves with its declaring type. ⚠ Type parameters are declined outright, which is what keeps generic math out: T.Zero where T is constrained to INumber<T> has the interface as its declaring type and the qualifier is not a class at all. dynamic, error types and an anonymous type qualifier are declined for the same reason. ⚠ An unqualified reference from inside the derived type is not this rule. Count written on its own inside Leaf is not a member access and never reaches the analyzer; only a written qualifier does. The fix replaces the qualifier with the declaring type, spelled short where that name binds to that type at the site and fully qualified where it does not, and is withheld where a comment or a preprocessor directive sits in the span. fixIsSafe: true: the two spellings resolve to the same member, so the edit changes nothing the program does. Generated code is excluded.
